interactive.title: One current: field, torque, speed
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Eight screens, with Back and Continue. One picture to play with, two quick choices and a card to keep. No marks and no timers.

Screen 1, How it works. A still drawing: a DC supply, then the series field winding drawn as a few turns of thick wire, then the armature between its brushes, all in one loop. One arrow runs round the loop, labelled "the same current through both". A curved arrow on the armature shows it turning, and a label "back-emf" points against the supply. The words beside it: "You already know one. An angle grinder's motor[^21] is a series motor built to run on AC as well.[^20] The field winding is in series with the armature. So one current flows through both.[^11] Torque comes from the field acting on the armature current. Here both are that one current. So more current means a stronger field and much more torque. A turning armature is a generator too. It makes a back-emf that opposes the supply. A stronger field or a faster spin makes more of it. At standstill there is none, so the starting current is large.[^1] Once it runs, the back-emf settles just under the supply voltage. The small gap pushes the current through the resistance: E = V − I R." Back-emf is the key term, marked in amber.

Screen 2, One current: field, torque, speed. The picture to play with. At the top, screen 1's loop redrawn small, with the armature's shaft driving a hoist drum through gears. Beside the field winding, a bar for the field's strength, full at 2.00. Below it, a bar for the back-emf, which stays full: it always matches the supply. The armature turns at a pace in step with the speed readout, slowed right down. The load on the drum's rope grows and shrinks with the torque. Below, a plot against load current, from 0.25 to 2.00 per unit. Two curves, drawn in full: torque, rising as the current squared, and speed, falling as one over the current. The axis runs from 0 to 4.00. Over the light-load half of the plot, up to full load, a band above 3.00 is shaded red and labelled "speed danger line: an example, not a maker's". A dot on each curve sits at the slider's value. Then one row of three readouts, on a phone too: Field, per unit. Torque, per unit. Speed, per unit. The speed readout turns red above 3.00. On a laptop the plot sits beside the motor.

The control. Load current: a slider from 0.25 to 2.00 per unit of full-load current, in steps of 0.05. It starts at 1.00, full load.

The rule it computes, for an ideal series motor: no saturation, no resistance, no friction. Everything is per unit, so 1.00 is full-load current, torque and speed. Field = current. Torque = field × current = current².[^3] Speed = one over the field = one over the current.[^12] That is because the back-emf goes with field × speed and stays equal to the supply.

Worked on the screen, under the readouts:
At 2.00: field 2.00, torque 2.00 × 2.00 = 4.00, speed 1 ÷ 2.00 = 0.50.
At 0.50: field 0.50, torque 0.50 × 0.50 = 0.25, speed 1 ÷ 0.50 = 2.00.
At 0.25: field 0.25, torque 0.25 × 0.25 = 0.0625, about 0.06, speed 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.00.
The speed crosses the red line near 0.33, a third of full-load current.

The words on the screen, above the picture: "Assume an ideal series motor, with no saturation and no resistance. 1.00 is full load. The red line at 3.00 is an example, not a maker's limit." The prompt above the picture: "Drag the load current up and down and watch the field, the torque and the speed." The caption under the readouts gives the cause at each setting, for example at 0.50: "At 0.50 of full-load current the field is 0.50. Torque is field times current, so it is 0.25. The back-emf must still match the supply. In a weaker field the armature must spin faster to make it. So the speed is 2.00." Read: At full load the field, torque and speed all read 1.00. At twice the current, as at a hard start, the torque is four times, 4.00, and the speed halves to 0.50. At half the current the field halves. The torque falls to a quarter, 0.25. The speed doubles to 2.00. At a quarter of the current the torque is only 0.06 and the speed is 4.00, deep in the red. All the while the back-emf bar stays full. The speed crosses the example danger line near a third of full-load current. Still: the slider at 0.25, the field bar an eighth full, the back-emf bar full, the load small, the dots at torque 0.06 and speed 4.00 in the red band, and the readouts 0.25, 0.06 and 4.00 with the speed in red.

Screen 3, Check on the cause. "A hoist is lifting on a DC series motor. The coupling shears and the load comes off. What does the motor do?" Three choices, in this order: "It slows and stops: it has nothing to drive"; "It speeds up a little, then holds a steady speed"; "Its speed climbs and keeps climbing". Right, the third: "Right. With no load it speeds up, and the current falls. Less current means a weaker field. In a weaker field the armature must spin faster to make the same back-emf. So it speeds up again, and keeps climbing.[^13] That is runaway. It is why the motor must have overspeed protection.[^2]" Wrong, the first: "It still has its supply. With no load the current falls and the field weakens. A weaker field means more speed, not less." Wrong, the second: "That is how an induction motor behaves, held just under synchronous speed. A series motor has no such speed. Its field weakens with the current, so it keeps speeding up." After a wrong choice, the right answer and its reason. Runaway is the key term, marked in amber.

Screen 4, How it behaves. A still drawing: screen 2's two curves without the slider, labelled "sketch from the ideal rule". Rows, each with a label.

Starting torque: "Very high. Torque goes with current squared until the iron saturates.[^3] After that, it goes with current alone."

Speed: "Poor regulation. The speed changes a lot with load. With no load it climbs dangerously."

Starting current: "At standstill only the resistance limits it. A 260 V motor with a 0.4 Ω armature would take 650 A. That is about twelve times full load.[^4] The field's resistance makes the real figure a little less. So it starts through a starting resistance."

Reversing: "Swap the field leads or the armature leads, not both.[^5] Swapping the supply leads leaves it turning the same way."

Screen 5, Where it is used, and its limits. A still drawing: the motor driving a hoist drum through gears, labelled "geared, never belted". Rows.

Used for: "Crane hoists, lifts and large excavators, where big starting torque matters. Also traction, such as railway locomotives."

History: "In 1907 the US Navy used series motors on boat cranes, for their starting torque.[^6]"

Coupling: "Couple it directly or through gears. Then the load is far less likely to come off. Never use a belt, which can break.[^7]"

Protection: "It must have overspeed protection.[^2] Its starter has a no-load release that lets go if the current falls."

Screen 6, Faults and tests. A still drawing: the isolator open with a lock and tag on it, a megger on the windings to frame, and the brushes on the commutator. Rows.

Safety first: "Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you touch the motor or its starter."

It races: "The load came off. Find out why, and check the overspeed trip."

Sparking: "Worn brushes or a pitted commutator. Poor contact makes them spark."

Will not start: "Look for an open field, a lead to earth, or poor brush contact."

Tests: "Megger the windings to frame. Measure the armature and field resistance.[^8]"

Screen 7, Find the fault. "A ventilation fan runs on a DC series motor. One day the motor suddenly races and trips on overspeed. What is the most likely fault?" Three choices, in this order: "The field winding has gone open circuit"; "The drive belt has snapped"; "The brushes are worn". Right, the second: "Right. A snapped belt leaves the motor with no load. The current fell, the field weakened and the speed climbed. The fix is a direct or geared drive, not a new belt.[^7]" Wrong, the first: "In a series motor the field carries the armature current. Open it and no current flows, so the motor stops. It cannot race." Wrong, the third: "Worn brushes cause sparking and poor contact. They make a motor weak or slow to start, not race." After a wrong choice, the right answer and its reason.

Screen 8, Keep this: the summary card, drawn from the lesson's summary with no case figures, then Finish the lesson.

Every figure on these screens is a control, worked from a rule shown, a cited value or a labelled example. The red line at 3.00 is an example, not a maker's limit.
interactive.ignores: The picture is an ideal series motor: no saturation, no resistance and no friction. On it, the speed with no load at all has no limit. A real motor's losses do set a limit. That limit can be past the point of damage. Past saturation the field stops growing, so torque goes with the current alone. Resistance makes the real speed a little lower under heavy load. Everything is per unit, not a real motor's rpm or newton metres.

explain.text:
A DC series motor has its field winding in series with the armature. So one current flows through both. Torque comes from the field acting on the armature current. Here both are that one current. So below saturation, torque goes with the current squared. Double the current and you get four times the torque. That is why it starts so hard.

A turning armature is a generator too. It makes a [[back-emf]] that opposes the supply. Like any generator, it makes more with a stronger field or a faster spin. At standstill there is none, so only the windings' resistance limits the current. As the motor speeds up, the back-emf rises and the current falls. It settles where the back-emf is just under the supply voltage.

Now take the load off. The motor speeds up, the back-emf rises and the current falls. But less current means a weaker field. A weaker field makes less back-emf at the same speed. So the motor speeds up again. Below saturation and ignoring resistance, the speed goes with one over the current. At half the current it doubles. With no load it can keep climbing until it damages itself. That is [[runaway]]. The picture shows this ideal case, with no saturation or resistance. Real curves bend, but the speed still climbs as the load falls.

**One current makes both the field and the torque. So torque climbs with the current squared. Take the load off and the speed climbs dangerously.**

analogy.text: Think of an automatic gearbox that changes gear by load alone. Heavy load, and it drops to a low gear: slow and strong. Light load, and it changes up: fast and weak. A series motor does the same by itself, because its field follows the load current.
analogy.breaks: A gearbox has a top gear and the engine has a rev limiter. A series motor has neither built in. As the load falls it keeps changing up, so with no load it can run away.

practice.text:
- Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you touch the motor or its starter.
- Check the drive. It must be direct or through gears, never a belt.
- Check that overspeed protection is fitted.
- Megger the windings to frame.
- Measure the armature and field resistance. An open circuit means a broken winding or connection.
- Look at the brushes and commutator for wear, pitting and sparking.
- Only then restore the supply and start it through its starter. Never bypass the starting resistance.

**Rule of thumb:** with no starter, the first current is the supply voltage over the resistance. That is many times full load.

**Worked example:** take a 260 V motor with a 0.4 Ω armature. At standstill there is no back-emf. So I = 260 ÷ 0.4 = 650 A, about twelve times its full-load current.[^4] The series field adds a little resistance, so the real figure is slightly less. A starting resistance in series with the armature brings that down. Starters typically keep it to 125 to 200% of full load.[^9] Some aim for two or three times.[^10]

**Common mistakes**
- Running it on test with the load uncoupled. A series motor cannot run safely with no load.
- Swapping the supply leads to reverse it. That reverses field and armature together, so it turns the same way.
- Expecting torque to go with current squared at every load. Past saturation it goes with current alone.
- Fitting a new belt after a belt failure. Change to a direct or geared drive.

summary.title: The DC series motor
summary.for: Loads that need big starting torque and stay coupled. One current feeds field and armature. So torque climbs steeply with current. Take the load off and it runs away.
summary.rule:
One current through field and armature.
Back-emf: E = V − I R. R is the armature plus the series field. Zero at standstill.
Below saturation: torque goes with I².
Ignoring resistance: speed goes with 1 ÷ I.
Past saturation: torque goes with I.
No starter: I = V ÷ R. 260 V ÷ 0.4 Ω = 650 A, about twelve times full load. The field's resistance makes the real figure a little less.

Very high starting torque. Poor speed regulation.
A starting resistance limits the starting current, typically to 125 to 200% of full load. Some aim for two to three times. Use the maker's setting.
Reverse it by swapping the field or the armature leads, not both.

traps.text: Never run it unloaded or drive through a belt. Couple it directly or through gears.
Lose the load and it runs away. It must have overspeed protection.
At standstill there is no back-emf. Only the resistance limits the current, so start it through its starter.
Swapping the supply leads does not reverse it. Swap the field or the armature leads.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead. Then megger to frame, measure field and armature resistance, and check the brushes and commutator.

summary.where: Crane hoists, lifts, large excavators and traction.

interactive.title: One current: field, torque, speed
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the field weaken, the torque fall with the current squared and the speed climb into the red when you drag the load current down.

checks.label: Full load gives field, torque and speed 1.00; twice the current gives 2.00, 4.00 and 0.50; half the current gives 0.50, 0.25 and 2.00; a quarter gives 0.25, 0.06 and 4.00; the speed crosses 3.00 near 0.33, so 0.30 is past it at 3.33 and 0.35 under it at 2.86
As the load current falls the field falls with it, the torque falls faster than the field, and the speed always rises; field × speed stays 1.00, so the back-emf stays equal to the supply
The developed torque is proportional to the square of the armature current: double the current, four times the torque
For a series motor the speed is inversely proportional to the armature current: half the current, twice the speed
A motor with an armature resistance of 0.4 ohms on a 260 V DC supply would draw 650 A at start

applied.problem: Speed going with one over the current holds only below saturation as well as ignoring resistance; and 'keeps climbing until the motor can damage itself' is stated as certain, where the sources say it can rise to dangerous levels and losses set some limit.

The checklist starts the motor before the megger and resistance tests, which need it still isolated; the 650 A case is a general DC motor, so a series field's resistance lowers it a little; and the source's 'typically' 125 to 200% was stated as what starters do.
The card gives one guide's 125 to 200% as the rule, though the lesson's sources differ (two to three times by another guide); a card read alone must keep both.
'A series motor has neither' clashes with the lesson's own overspeed protection, a fitted rev limiter; and 'it runs away' is stated as certain where the sources say it can.

Screen 5 says a direct or geared coupling means the load 'cannot come off', but screen 3's own coupling shears; a coupling makes losing the load far less likely, not impossible. The built screen 5 needs the same words.

notes.problem: The built interactive's screen 5 'Coupling' row still reads 'so the load cannot come off'; it should read 'so the load is far less likely to come off', to match the corrected description and screen 3's sheared coupling.
